structure.title: **Abstract**
structure.text:
The solid solution La Li TiO (0.03 , *<sup>x</sup>* , 0.167) has been investigated by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD), 2/32*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup>*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup> <sup>7</sup> impedance spectroscopy (IS) and Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques. In these samples, a change of symmetry from tetragonal to orthorhombic is observed when the lithium content is decreased below *x* 5 0.06. Structural modifications produced are mainly due to cation vacancies ordering along the *<sup>c</sup>*-axis, which disappear gradually when the Li <sup>7</sup> content increases. Two Li signals with different quadrupole constants are detected in Li NMR spectra of orthorhombic/ tetragonal perovskites, which have been associated with two crystallographic sites. In La Li TiO perovskite, prepared by 0.5 0.5 3 <sup>7</sup> quenching from 13008C into liquid nitrogen, an important mobility for Li was detected in Li NMR spectra. In perovskites analysed, the dependence of electrical conductivity on Li content departs from that expected on the basis of a random distribution of La and Li in A sites. Dc conductivity increases quickly with the Li content in orthorhombic samples, but changes much more smoothly in tetragonal ones, where vacancies distribution becomes progressively disordered. In all perovskites analysed, the dependence of dc-conductivity with temperature displays a non-Arrhenius behaviour, with activation energies of 0.3960.02 and 0.2960.02 eV in 160–250 and 250–360 K temperature ranges respectively. 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. For samples with high lithium contents (x=0.146 and 0.167), XRD patterns could be indexed with the diagonal perovskite cell ( $\sqrt{2}a_p \times \sqrt{2}a_p \times 2a_p$ ) deduced in a previous microstructural study [16]. However, the average crystal structure deduced from XRD experiments could be interpreted with a smaller cell. The best fitting of the XRD patterns was achieved using a primitive P4/mmm tetragonal cell, derived from the cubic perovskite, with  $a \approx a_p \approx 3.87$  Å and  $c \approx 2a_p$  [2,4,12]. In these samples, peaks associated with the doubled cell, labelled with asterisks in Fig. 1, are broad while those of the cubic sublattice are narrower.

For samples with low lithium content, x < 0.0625 the XRD patterns are slightly different. Splittings of different peaks have been detected, in particular,  $\{200\}$  lines became into three components (see inset of the Fig. 1), indicating the presence of an orthorhombic distortion in the perovskite network. All peaks of the XRD patterns were indexed with the *Pmmm* space group, and the unit cell parameters

were  $a \approx a_p \approx 3.864$  Å,  $b \approx a_p \approx 3.875$  Å,  $c \approx 2a_p \approx 7.786$  Å [17]. Note that, in the case of orthorhombic perovskites, peaks of the superstructure are sharper and stronger than those detected in tetragonal phases. In the case of tetragonal samples with x = 0.167, a fast cooling from 1350°C produced an XRD pattern without superstructure peaks (Fig. 2) that could be indexed with a cubic cell ( $a \approx 3.87$  Å).

nodes.title: Figure 1 and XRD Results for High Lithium Content
nodes.text: __IMG_01d9f318__ Fig. 1. Powder X-ray diffraction patterns of La Li TiO perovskites for four different compositions: 2/32*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup>*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup> *x*50.03, *x*50.063, *x*50.146 and *x*50.167. Superstructure peaks corresponding to the doubled perovskite are labelled with asterisks in the X-ray pattern of the *x*50.167 perovskite. Splitting of the (200) reflections are shown as insets. 0.146 and x = 0.167. Two different patterns can be obtained depending on the lithium content of these perovskites. For samples with high lithium contents (x=0.146 and 0.167), XRD patterns could be indexed with the diagonal perovskite cell ( $\sqrt{2}a_p \times \sqrt{2}a_p \times 2a_p$ ) deduced in a previous microstructural study [16]. However, the average crystal structure deduced from XRD experiments could be interpreted with a smaller cell. The best fitting of the XRD patterns was achieved using a primitive P4/mmm tetragonal cell, derived from the cubic perovskite, with  $a \approx a_p \approx 3.87$  Å and  $c \approx 2a_p$ [2,4,12]. In these samples, peaks associated with the doubled cell, labelled with asterisks in Fig. 1, are broad while those of the cubic sublattice are narrower.

nodes.title: XRD Results for Low Lithium Content and Orthorhombic Distortion
nodes.text:
For samples with low lithium content, x < 0.0625 the XRD patterns are slightly different. Splittings of different peaks have been detected, in particular,  $\{200\}$  lines became into three components (see inset of the Fig. 1), indicating the presence of an orthorhombic distortion in the perovskite network. All peaks of the XRD patterns were indexed with the *Pmmm* space group, and the unit cell parameters

were  $a \approx a_p \approx 3.864$  Å,  $b \approx a_p \approx 3.875$  Å,  $c \approx 2a_p \approx 7.786$  Å [17]. Note that, in the case of orthorhombic perovskites, peaks of the superstructure are sharper and stronger than those detected in tetragonal phases. In the case of tetragonal samples with x = 0.167, a fast cooling from 1350°C produced an XRD pattern without superstructure peaks (Fig. 2) that could be indexed with a cubic cell ( $a \approx 3.87$  Å).

structure.title: 3.2. <sup>7</sup>Li NMR experiments
structure.text:
$^7$ Li NMR spectra of La $_{2/3-x}$ Li $_{3x}$ TiO $_3$  perovskites, recorded at room temperature are shown in Fig. 3. The spectra are formed by an important central (-1/2, 1/2) transition and two broad and small  $(\pm 1/2, \pm 3/2)$  components, which are symmetrically disposed with respect to the central one.

A deeper analysis of NMR spectra of orthorhombic samples (x < 0.06) shows the existence of two Li NMR components, with different quadrupole constants ( $C_Q \approx 80$  and 0 kHz), whose relative intensities agree with those deduced from the structural analysis [17]. In tetragonal samples (x > 0.1), quadrupole constants decrease considerably ( $C_Q \approx 40$  and 0 kHz)

![](_page_3_Figure_9.jpeg)

Fig. 2. XRD patterns of the La<sub>0.5</sub>Li<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> perovskite, (a) quenched and (b) slowly cooled from 1350°C. Arrows denote superstructure peaks of the perovskite.

![](_page_4_Figure_2.jpeg)

<sup>7</sup> Fig. 3. Li NMR spectra of La Li TiO perovskites, recorded at room temperature. Quadrupole outer transitions, labelled with 2/32*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup>*<sup>x</sup>* <sup>3</sup> asterisks, are only clearly visible in orthorhombic samples. In tetragonal samples outer transition are responsible for the broad component detected at the resonance frequency.

and resolution of two components became difficult because of Li exchange processes. Finally, in tetragonal samples quenched from 13508C, quadrupole

patterns were almost undetectable (*<sup>C</sup>* ¯0 kHz). <sup>Q</sup> <sup>7</sup> The central component of the Li MAS NMR spectra displays a gaussian shape in orthorhombic samples but a lorentzian shape in tetragonal ones, indicating that the lithium mobility increases. Finally, in tetragonal samples quenched from 13508C, the width of the central line decreases indicating an additional increase of Li mobility (see insets of Fig. 3).

structure.title: Abstract / Introduction
structure.text:
The XRD patterns indexing of samples  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$ , 0.04 < x < 0.17, has shown that the unit cell symmetry changes from orthorhombic to tetragonal as Li content is increased. In Fig. 5, dependence of the lattice parameters on the Li content, x, of perovskites is given. A drop of the

![](_page_5_Figure_5.jpeg)

Fig. 5. Plot of the lattice parameters (top) and unit cell volume (bottom) versus Li content in  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  perovskites. Uncertainties on unit cell parameters are given in Table 2.

c-parameter is observed for  $x > \approx 0.06$ . In orthorhombic to tetragonal transformation, a and b parameters become similar and unit cell volume decreases. For high lithium contents, the c/2a ratio reaches values close to 1, and XRD pattern can be described with a cubic cell. Similar observations have been reported in the (1-x) CaTiO<sub>3</sub> - x La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> solid solution [18].

At present, the crystal chemistry of lithium lanthanum titanates has not been established. In this sense, different groups [5,12,19] have found similar results in the compositional range 0.04 < x < 0.15; however, results out of this range are scarce. In these studies, XRD patterns were interpreted on the basis of a tetragonal cell (space group P4/mmm), and in the case of Robertson et al. [5], two tetragonal cells, with different c/a ratio, were obtained for high and low lithium contents. Last authors reported also the existence of a cubic phase in the high temperature domain of the 'Li<sub>0.5</sub>La<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub>'-'La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub>' phase diagram.

In this study the splitting of {200} lines has been associated with a orthorhombic distortion of the perovskite. This distortion has been previously reported in oxygen-deficient perovskites La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3-8</sub>,  $0.07 \le \delta \le 0.079$ , by Abe and Uchino [20], Kim et al. [21] and MacEachern et al. [22]. These authors concluded that the observed double unit cell was produced by the ordered arrangement of La and vacancies along c-axis. The same type of La arrangebeen proposed for tetragonal  $La_{2/3-x}Li_{3x}TiO_3$  perovskites [5,12,17,19]; however, the orthorhombic splitting has been never detected, and is related to an additional distortion of the octahedral network.

In a second stage of this study, XRD patterns were analysed by means of the Rietveld method. In each sample, a structural refinement was done using the two proposed *P4/mmm* and *Pmmm* structural models [11,17,21] (Table 1). In each case, the refinement with the best agreement factors was retained. In this analysis, lithium contribution to XRD patterns was not considered due to its low scattering factor; La contents deduced from Rietveld analysis coincides within 10% with nominal ones. Structural parameters obtained from this analysis are given in Table 2. La ions exhibit a clear preference for (0, 0, 0) with respect to (0, 0, 1/2) positions, but this preference

In this case, samples quenched from 1350°C display a pseudocubic (space group Pm3m) symmetry and La and Li ions are randomly accommodated in a single site. Samples studied by Fourquet et al. [12] displayed the same trend; however, these au-

thors did not study the full disordered pole because of the narrower compositional range analysed.

In  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  series, titanium ions are displaced from the centre of polyhedra towards  $z\!=\!0.5$  layer, as deduced from the analysis of Ti–O interatomic distances (Fig. 6b). This fact can be explained on the basis of an asymmetric distribution of charge around the octahedra, produced by the alternating disposition of La and vacancies in contiguous planes of the perovskite. From this fact, one of the Ti–O distances becomes shorter while other ones get longer along the c-axis, producing the mentioned distortion of the TiO $_6$  octahedra. This distortion decreases when La ions become disordered. In the case of perovskites with  $x\!=\!0.167$ , La ions distribution is completely disordered and octahedra are almost regular.

Li NMR spectra of the orthorhombic (x < 0.06) and tetragonal (x > 0.08) samples exhibit small but appreciable differences. Structural distortions produced during cation ordering increase the electric field gradient at sites occupied by Li ions favouring detection of the quadrupole pattern. narrow line detected near the resonance frequencies corresponds to Li atoms with an important degree of mobility  $(C_0 \approx 0)$ , while the broad ones correspond to Li with a lower mobility ( $C_0 \approx 80$  kHz) [17]. Relative intensities of the two components agrees with those deduced from the structural analysis of these perovskites: the broad component has been associated with Li located at z/c=0 (30%) and the narrow line to Li located at z/c = 0.5 planes (70%), where vacancies are preferentially located. In tetragonal perovskites, a small broad non-resolved pattern was detected near the central transitions with  $C_0$  $\leq$ 40 kHz. In samples quenched from 1350°C, with  $x \ge 0.1$ , the intensity and the splitting of the quadrupole pattern decrease, being difficult its detection in <sup>7</sup>Li NMR spectra. In the last samples, a considerable narrowing of the central line is produced, indicating that mobility of Li is important.

With regard to electrical conductivity, dc-conductivity depends on lanthanum and vacancies distribution. It is generally assumed that ionic transport in these materials results from lithium ions hopping to near vacant A sites [2,3,23,24]. Therefore, two factors mainly affect the ionic conductivity: the carrier concentration and the probability of ions hopping to neighbor vacant sites. In a first approximation, the effective carrier concentration should be equal to the product  $n_c n_v$ , where  $n_c$  is the lithium and  $n_y$  is the vacant A sites concentrations. NMR spin-lattice relaxation and electrical conductivity relaxation rates measured on end members of these perovskites showed that all lithium participates in the ionic ac-conductivity [23–25]. However, some discrepancies between predicted and observed values have been detected that makes the proposed model inadequate. In particular, a random distribution of Li and vacancies on A sites would give conductivity values near zero for x=0  $(n_0=0)$  and x=0.167 $(n_y = 0)$ . In orthorhombic samples, conductivity values increase with  $n_c$  in the predicted way. However in tetragonal samples, with high Li contents, conductivity values are always important, suggesting that the amount of vacancies implicated in conductivity must be much higher that considered in this model. This hypothesis has been confirmed in a recent neutron diffraction study of La<sub>0.5</sub>Li<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> perovskite, where Li ions have been located at the centre of the cube faces of the primitive perovskite (1/6 occupancy), instead of the A site [26]. In the resulting rhombohedral R3c perovskite, the amount of vacancies to which Li can hop is clearly higher than assumed in previous works.

The accommodation of cation vacancies in alternating planes along the {001} axis should favours a two-dimensional movement of Li in orthorhombic samples [17,19]. However, in tetragonal samples, cation and vacancies turn progressively disordered favouring a three-dimensional movement of Li. Associated with vacancies disordering, a considerable narrowing of the central line is produced, indicating a substantial increment on the mobility of Li along the series. All these facts explain the trend observed on the ionic conductivity of perovskites, in which ionic conductivity increases with the lithium

content, up to the maximum detected at  $x \approx 0.13$  in tetragonal perovskites.

In a previous study, it was shown that, successive high temperatures quenching and annealing treatments changed vacancies distribution in tetragonal perovskites. These treatments were responsible for an enhancement of ionic conductivity, by a factor about 2, on quenched samples respect to annealed ones [13,27]. All described observations point to that ionic conductivity of the series  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  depends also on the vacancies distribution.

On the other hand, it has also been observed that structural parameters change only slightly with the Li content. From this fact, it would be expected that the necessary energy by lithium ions to hop into a near A site, should remain almost unchanged. This point has been experimentally confirmed in perovskites with different symmetry, where the same temperature dependence of conductivity has been observed, and activation energies deduced for Li motion changes only slightly along the series. In order to explain the behaviour of these perovskites, additional work must be done.

nodes.title: Review of Previous Studies on Crystal Chemistry
nodes.text: For high lithium contents, the c/2a ratio reaches values close to 1, and XRD pattern can be described with a cubic cell. Similar observations have been reported in the (1-x) CaTiO<sub>3</sub> - x La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> solid solution [18]. At present, the crystal chemistry of lithium lanthanum titanates has not been established. In this sense, different groups [5,12,19] have found similar results in the compositional range 0.04 < x < 0.15; however, results out of this range are scarce. In these studies, XRD patterns were interpreted on the basis of a tetragonal cell (space group P4/mmm), and in the case of Robertson et al. [5], two tetragonal cells, with different c/a ratio, were obtained for high and low lithium contents. Last authors reported also the existence of a cubic phase in the high temperature domain of the 'Li<sub>0.5</sub>La<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub>'-'La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub>' phase diagram. In this study the splitting of {200} lines has been associated with a orthorhombic distortion of the perovskite. This distortion has been previously reported in oxygen-deficient perovskites La<sub>2/3</sub>TiO<sub>3-8</sub>,  $0.07 \le \delta \le 0.079$ , by Abe and Uchino [20], Kim et al. [21] and MacEachern et al. [22]. These authors concluded that the observed double unit cell was produced by the ordered arrangement of La and vacancies along c-axis. The same type of La arrangebeen proposed for tetragonal  $La_{2/3-x}Li_{3x}TiO_3$  perovskites [5,12,17,19]; however, the orthorhombic splitting has been never detected, and is related to an additional distortion of the octahedral network.

nodes.title: Rietveld Analysis: Cation Ordering and Octahedral Distortions
nodes.text:
In a second stage of this study, XRD patterns were analysed by means of the Rietveld method. In each sample, a structural refinement was done using the two proposed *P4/mmm* and *Pmmm* structural models [11,17,21] (Table 1). In each case, the refinement with the best agreement factors was retained. In this analysis, lithium contribution to XRD patterns was not considered due to its low scattering factor; La contents deduced from Rietveld analysis coincides within 10% with nominal ones. Structural parameters obtained from this analysis are given in Table 2. La ions exhibit a clear preference for (0, 0, 0) with respect to (0, 0, 1/2) positions, but this preference

Table 1
Positional parameters for tetragonal and orthorhombic perovskites used in the structural refinement (Li has not been considered in the refinement) __TBL_bf60ca0a__ $<sup>^{</sup>a}$  Taken from Ref. [12] for  $La_{2/3-x}Li_{3x}TiO_{3}$  system.

decreases as the Li content increases (Fig. 6a). La ions distribution becomes completely disordered in tetragonal perovskites with Li content near to x = 0.167. In this case, samples quenched from 1350°C display a pseudocubic (space group Pm3m) symmetry and La and Li ions are randomly accommodated in a single site. Samples studied by Fourquet et al. [12] displayed the same trend; however, these au-

thors did not study the full disordered pole because of the narrower compositional range analysed. In  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  series, titanium ions are displaced from the centre of polyhedra towards  $z\!=\!0.5$  layer, as deduced from the analysis of Ti–O interatomic distances (Fig. 6b). This fact can be explained on the basis of an asymmetric distribution of charge around the octahedra, produced by the alternating disposition of La and vacancies in contiguous planes of the perovskite. From this fact, one of the Ti–O distances becomes shorter while other ones get longer along the c-axis, producing the mentioned distortion of the TiO $_6$  octahedra. This distortion decreases when La ions become disordered. In the case of perovskites with  $x\!=\!0.167$ , La ions distribution is completely disordered and octahedra are almost regular.

narrow line detected near the resonance frequencies corresponds to Li atoms with an important degree of mobility  $(C_0 \approx 0)$ , while the broad ones correspond to Li with a lower mobility ( $C_0 \approx 80$  kHz) [17]. Relative intensities of the two components agrees with those deduced from the structural analysis of these perovskites: the broad component has been associated with Li located at z/c=0 (30%) and the narrow line to Li located at z/c = 0.5 planes (70%), where vacancies are preferentially located. In tetragonal perovskites, a small broad non-resolved pattern was detected near the central transitions with  $C_0$  $\leq$ 40 kHz. In samples quenched from 1350°C, with  $x \ge 0.1$ , the intensity and the splitting of the quadrupole pattern decrease, being difficult its detection in <sup>7</sup>Li NMR spectra. In the last samples, a considerable narrowing of the central line is produced, indicating that mobility of Li is important.

nodes.title: Electrical Conductivity and Ionic Transport Mechanism
nodes.text:
With regard to electrical conductivity, dc-conductivity depends on lanthanum and vacancies distribution. It is generally assumed that ionic transport in these materials results from lithium ions hopping to near vacant A sites [2,3,23,24]. Therefore, two factors mainly affect the ionic conductivity: the carrier concentration and the probability of ions hopping to neighbor vacant sites. In a first approximation, the effective carrier concentration should be equal to the product  $n_c n_v$ , where  $n_c$  is the lithium and  $n_y$  is the vacant A sites concentrations. NMR spin-lattice relaxation and electrical conductivity relaxation rates measured on end members of these perovskites showed that all lithium participates in the ionic ac-conductivity [23–25]. However, some discrepancies between predicted and observed values have been detected that makes the proposed model inadequate. In particular, a random distribution of Li and vacancies on A sites would give conductivity values near zero for x=0  $(n_0=0)$  and x=0.167 $(n_y = 0)$ . In orthorhombic samples, conductivity values increase with  $n_c$  in the predicted way. However in tetragonal samples, with high Li contents, conductivity values are always important, suggesting that the amount of vacancies implicated in conductivity must be much higher that considered in this model. This hypothesis has been confirmed in a recent neutron diffraction study of La<sub>0.5</sub>Li<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> perovskite, where Li ions have been located at the centre of the cube faces of the primitive perovskite (1/6 occupancy), instead of the A site [26]. In the resulting rhombohedral R3c perovskite, the amount of vacancies to which Li can hop is clearly higher than assumed in previous works. The accommodation of cation vacancies in alternating planes along the {001} axis should favours a two-dimensional movement of Li in orthorhombic samples [17,19]. However, in tetragonal samples, cation and vacancies turn progressively disordered favouring a three-dimensional movement of Li. Associated with vacancies disordering, a considerable narrowing of the central line is produced, indicating a substantial increment on the mobility of Li along the series. All these facts explain the trend observed on the ionic conductivity of perovskites, in which ionic conductivity increases with the lithium

content, up to the maximum detected at  $x \approx 0.13$  in tetragonal perovskites.

nodes.title: Influence of Thermal Treatments on Conductivity
nodes.text: In a previous study, it was shown that, successive high temperatures quenching and annealing treatments changed vacancies distribution in tetragonal perovskites. These treatments were responsible for an enhancement of ionic conductivity, by a factor about 2, on quenched samples respect to annealed ones [13,27]. All described observations point to that ionic conductivity of the series  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  depends also on the vacancies distribution. On the other hand, it has also been observed that structural parameters change only slightly with the Li content. From this fact, it would be expected that the necessary energy by lithium ions to hop into a near A site, should remain almost unchanged. This point has been experimentally confirmed in perovskites with different symmetry, where the same temperature dependence of conductivity has been observed, and activation energies deduced for Li motion changes only slightly along the series.

structure.title: 5. Conclusions
structure.text:
Structure and transport properties of the  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  (0.03 $\leq$ x $\leq$ 0.167) solid solution have been investigated. Most of analysed perovskites exhibit a double unit cell ( $a_p \times a_p \times 2a_p$ ), the symmetry changing from orthorhombic to tetragonal when the Li content increases above x=0.06. In Li poor samples, La ions and vacancies alternate in contiguous planes along the c-axis. Distribution of vacancies becomes progressively disordered when the Li content increases, being completely disordered in Li-rich samples quenched from high temperatures (1350°C).

In the NMR study of  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  samples, two types of perovskites have been distinguished in accordance with the XRD study. In orthorhombic perovskites, two types of Li, with different mobility, have been ascribed to Li located in two planes of the perovskite. Li with low mobility, located at z/c=0 planes, display important quadrupole constants ( $C_Q=0.80~\text{kHz}$ ) and Li with a high mobility, located at z/c=0.5~planes, display small constants ( $C_Q=0~\text{kHz}$ ). In tetragonal and cubic phases, quadrupole

constants decrease and resolution of two sites becomes more difficult. The increase of Li mobility along the series is the responsible for the progressive line narrowing of the central transition detected in <sup>7</sup>Li spectra.

Electrical conductivity increases with lithium content in orthorhombic samples but displays only a weak dependence in tetragonal ones. High values of conductivity measured in samples with x>0.13 require a higher amount of vacancies that considered in the random distribution model of La and vacancies. This fact was recently confirmed by neutron diffraction experiments on the  $La_{0.5}Li_{0.5}TiO_3$  end member, where an unusual position for Li was detected [26]. In all samples analysed, a non-Arrhenius dependence of dc-conductivity with temperature was obtained.

nodes.title: Structural Properties
nodes.text: Structure and transport properties of the  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  (0.03 $\leq$ x $\leq$ 0.167) solid solution have been investigated. Most of analysed perovskites exhibit a double unit cell ( $a_p \times a_p \times 2a_p$ ), the symmetry changing from orthorhombic to tetragonal when the Li content increases above x=0.06. In Li poor samples, La ions and vacancies alternate in contiguous planes along the c-axis. Distribution of vacancies becomes progressively disordered when the Li content increases, being completely disordered in Li-rich samples quenched from high temperatures (1350°C).

nodes.title: NMR Study and Lithium Mobility
nodes.text:
In the NMR study of  $\text{La}_{2/3-x}\text{Li}_{3x}\text{TiO}_3$  samples, two types of perovskites have been distinguished in accordance with the XRD study. In orthorhombic perovskites, two types of Li, with different mobility, have been ascribed to Li located in two planes of the perovskite. Li with low mobility, located at z/c=0 planes, display important quadrupole constants ( $C_Q=0.80~\text{kHz}$ ) and Li with a high mobility, located at z/c=0.5~planes, display small constants ( $C_Q=0~\text{kHz}$ ). In tetragonal and cubic phases, quadrupole

constants decrease and resolution of two sites becomes more difficult. The increase of Li mobility along the series is the responsible for the progressive line narrowing of the central transition detected in <sup>7</sup>Li spectra.

nodes.title: Electrical Conductivity
nodes.text: Electrical conductivity increases with lithium content in orthorhombic samples but displays only a weak dependence in tetragonal ones. High values of conductivity measured in samples with x>0.13 require a higher amount of vacancies that considered in the random distribution model of La and vacancies. This fact was recently confirmed by neutron diffraction experiments on the  $La_{0.5}Li_{0.5}TiO_3$  end member, where an unusual position for Li was detected [26]. In all samples analysed, a non-Arrhenius dependence of dc-conductivity with temperature was obtained.
